bull_bear.body:
- Part of the JSW Group since 2022 and a subsidiary of JSW Cement, giving access to advanced technologies, a wider distribution network and capital resources
- Acts as a key feeder to the Group's eastern plants, providing demand visibility and supply-chain efficiency
- Captive limestone mines plus proximity to limestone, slag and fly ash supporting cost-efficient production
- Strategic location at the intersection of Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand with access to eastern Indian markets
- Logistics connectivity: 2 km from the Rourkela-Jharsuguda state highway, railway stations at Sagra (~24 km) and Sonakhan (~19 km), plus a newly commissioned dedicated railway siding at Sagra
- Energy efficiency from an 8.9 MW WHRS meeting ~60% of the clinker plant's power requirement
- Forward integration after the 1 MTPA grinding unit, with products routed through JSW Cement's established distribution network
- Zero Lost Time Injuries in FY 2025-26, recognised with a Merit category award from the British Safety Council
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Industry supply-demand mismatch — The MD&A's risk table states the cement sector is prone to supply-demand mismatches and faces fluctuations in its end-user sectors; with the industry adding roughly 50-55 MTPA of capacity in FY 2025-26 and a further 42-44 MTPA planned for FY 2026-27, regional oversupply can compress realisations for a small eastern-India producer.
- Raw material availability and quality (limestone) — Management flags that production is constrained by difficulties in sourcing sufficient, suitable-quality limestone; the Company mitigates through captive mines, auctioned mines, strategic inventory and specialist consultants for limestone deposit utilisation plans, but limestone availability is also cited industry-wide as a constraint on capacity addition.
- Input and energy cost volatility (coal, pet coke, fuel) — The stated raw-material risk is continual margin erosion from volatile input costs, with rising global prices for coal and pet coke directly increasing manufacturing expenditure. Geopolitical tension in West Asia raised crude, pet coke, imported coal and diesel costs during the year; management says these pressures intensified late in FY 2025-26 and are expected to persist in the near term.
- Infrastructure and logistics constraints — The Company states the cement industry is highly exposed to logistical inefficiencies, with higher freight costs and inadequate critical infrastructure, particularly rail freight capacity and last-mile connectivity. Mitigation rests on the newly commissioned Sagra railway siding and the planned limestone belt conveyor, both still to prove savings.
- Leverage and negative net worth — The MD&A ratio commentary notes debt increased due to availment of a fresh term loan for project activity together with equity erosion, resulting in negative net worth for the year, and flags a DBS Bank term loan bullet payment of Rs 201.50 Cr due in March 2027 - a concentrated refinancing/repayment event against a loss-making year and rising finance cost.
- Dependence on the JSW group for offtake, distribution and operations — The clinker plant is described as a key feeder to the Group's eastern plants; market presence is built on JSW Cement's established distribution network, the premium product is marketed by the parent as CHD Jalkavach, the 1 MTPA grinding capacity runs under an exclusive manufacturing partnership with group company Bhushan Power & Steel Limited, and CSR spending is borne by the holding company. Commercial terms and volumes are therefore substantially group-determined; the MD&A also notes there are no trade receivables as all sales are made against advance.
- Single-site, single-region concentration — Operations sit at one plant site at Village Telighana, Kutra, District Sundargarh, Odisha, with mines at Village Khatkurbahal, serving Odisha, West Bengal, Jharkhand and Bihar - so any disruption at the site, its mines or in eastern-India demand hits the entire business, and the new capacity is a single grinding unit at Sambalpur.
- Execution and ramp-up of the new capacity — FY 2026-27 earnings depend on maximising utilisation of the just-commissioned 1 MTPA grinding unit and on completing the belt conveyor project, which was still at pre-project activity stage; jobwork charges for operating the BPSL grinding unit already drove other expenses up 81.88%, so ramp shortfalls would leave the added cost without the volume.
- Environment, health & safety (EHS) and decarbonisation — The Company's own EHS risk entry states that growing environmental concerns and regulatory requirements on greenhouse gas emissions could limit its operations, and that the industry faces strict labour laws and health and safety regulations. Cement is among the most energy-intensive and carbon-emitting industrial processes, and the Company's Thermal Substitution Rate moderated during FY 2025-26 versus the prior year, leaving its alternative-fuel progress a live watch item.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: Shiva Cement, incorporated in Odisha in 1985 and a subsidiary of JSW Cement Limited (part of the JSW Group) since 2017, manufactures clinker and, from FY 2025-26, cement. Its manufacturing set-up comprises a clinkerisation plant, a cement grinding unit, a waste heat recovery power plant and captive limestone mines, with the clinker plant acting as a feeder to JSW Cement's eastern plants. The commissioning and ramp-up of a 1 MTPA grinding unit at Sambalpur enabled the transition from a pure clinker manufacturer to an integrated cement producer serving eastern Indian markets through JSW Cement's distribution network.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Clinker:** Clinker
- **Cement:** Cement (ground at the Sambalpur unit), CHD Jalkavach (premium offering marketed by parent JSW Cement), Portland Composite Cement (PCC) - planned blend
- **Minerals:** Dolomite (sales planned)
business.title: Products & brands

business.body:
- JSW Cement Limited — related party: Holding company of Shiva Cement; the clinker plant acts as a feeder to the Group's eastern plants and Shiva Cement's products are sold through JSW Cement's distribution network, with the premium offering marketed by the parent as CHD Jalkavach. JSW Cement also bore the CSR spending.
- Bhushan Power and Steel Limited (BPSL) — related party: Group company; partner in the exclusive manufacturing partnership under which the 1 MTPA cement grinding unit at Sambalpur, Odisha operates (commissioned 03 September 2025).

business.title: Competitive strengths

outlook.body:
- Shift focus from project execution to value creation in FY 2026-27, having substantially completed the major expansion projects
- Maximise utilisation of the newly commissioned 1 MTPA grinding unit at Sambalpur, Odisha, built in partnership with group company Bhushan Power and Steel Limited
- Complete and commission the belt conveyor system for limestone transport from mines to plant to lower logistics cost and carbon emissions
- Expand the portfolio of value-added products and commercialise dolomite sales as an additional revenue stream
- Leverage JSW Cement's expertise, distribution network and Group scale, with the clinker plant acting as a key feeder to the Group's eastern plants
- Strengthen the supply chain by increasing limestone sourcing from both existing and auctioned mines
- Sharpen focus on cost optimisation and operational efficiency in response to fuel, logistics and currency-driven cost pressures
- Advance sustainability by improving the clinker factor and thermal substitution rate and investing in renewable energy and Waste Heat Recovery Systems
- Expand the eastern India footprint and introduce blended cement variants such as Portland Composite Cement (PCC)
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 was the year Shiva Cement's multi-year investment cycle in clinker capacity expansion, infrastructure and downstream integration began to convert into operating outcomes. The landmark project of the year was the 1 MTPA cement grinding unit at Sambalpur, Odisha, commissioned on September 03, 2025 under an exclusive manufacturing partnership with group company Bhushan Power and Steel Limited (BPSL); its commissioning and ramp-up moved the Company from pure clinker manufacturing to integrated cement production alongside the existing 4,000 TPD (1.32 MTPA) clinkerisation plant that had commenced commercial operation in June 2023. The Company also commissioned a dedicated railway siding at Sagra for inward and outward movement in 2026. On the supply-chain side, limestone sourcing was increased from both existing and auctioned mines and significant progress was made on pre-project activities for a belt conveyor system to move limestone from the mines to the plant, a project management intends to complete and commission in FY 2026-27 and expects to lower logistics costs and carbon emissions. Under JSW Group's guidance the Company states it is poised to expand clinker capacity further and to introduce cement blends such as Portland Composite Cement (PCC). With major expansion projects substantially completed, FY 2026-27 priorities shift from project execution to value creation - maximising grinding-unit utilisation, expanding value-added products and commercialising dolomite sales. The MD&A notes that debt increased due to availment of a fresh term loan for project activity.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian real GDP growth projected at 6.8-7.2% for FY 2026-27, supported by sustained government infrastructure spending and rising private investment
- Union Budget 2026-27 public capital expenditure raised to Rs 12.2 lakh crore (3.1% of GDP), a 9% YoY increase, directed at highways, railways and urban transport - expected to generate multiplier effects for cement
- Indian cement consumption grew 6-7% in FY 2025-26 following 9.4% construction-sector growth in FY 2024-25; domestic demand expected at 495-502 million tonnes in FY 2026 and 670-680 million tonnes by FY 2030
- Housing remains the largest demand driver at over 55-57% of total cement consumption; India's per-capita consumption of ~290-340 kg versus a global average of 470-520 kg indicates substantial headroom
- Indian cement market valued at $21.0 billion in 2025, projected to reach $40.4 billion by 2034 (CAGR 7.52% over 2026-2034); India's installed capacity ~690 MTPA with ~50-55 MTPA of additions in FY 2025-26 and a further 42-44 MTPA planned for FY 2026-27
- Structural shift toward blended, low-carbon and green cement, with greater use of supplementary cementitious materials improving both cost efficiency and environmental performance
- Near-term environment characterised by demand moderation, cost volatility and evolving execution dynamics; cost pressures from global energy markets, logistics constraints and currency movements intensified late in the year and are expected to persist
- Geopolitical tension in West Asia raising pet coke, imported coal and diesel costs and lengthening transit times, pressuring production economics
- Limestone availability and delays in land acquisition continue to constrain industry capacity addition
- Company-specific lever: forward integration into cement after the grinding unit commissioning enables greater value realisation, wider market participation and customer reach across eastern India
- WHRS met approximately 60% of the clinker plant's power requirement, supporting energy cost efficiency

risks.risk: Execution and ramp-up of the new capacity
risks.note: FY 2026-27 earnings depend on maximising utilisation of the just-commissioned 1 MTPA grinding unit and on completing the belt conveyor project, which was still at pre-project activity stage; jobwork charges for operating the BPSL grinding unit already drove other expenses up 81.88%, so ramp shortfalls would leave the added cost without the volume.

The Company's own EHS risk entry states that growing environmental concerns and regulatory requirements on greenhouse gas emissions could limit its operations, and that the industry faces strict labour laws and health and safety regulations. Cement is among the most energy-intensive and carbon-emitting industrial processes, and the Company's Thermal Substitution Rate moderated during FY 2025-26 versus the prior year, leaving its alternative-fuel progress a live watch item.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Shiva Cement Limited is a JSW Cement subsidiary operating an integrated cement platform in eastern India, built around a 1.32 MTPA clinkerisation plant in Odisha.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Shiva Cement, incorporated in Odisha in 1985 and a subsidiary of JSW Cement Limited (part of the JSW Group) since 2017, manufactures clinker and, from FY 2025-26, cement. Its manufacturing set-up comprises a clinkerisation plant, a cement grinding unit, a waste heat recovery power plant and captive limestone mines, with the clinker plant acting as a feeder to JSW Cement's eastern plants. The commissioning and ramp-up of a 1 MTPA grinding unit at Sambalpur enabled the transition from a pure clinker manufacturer to an integrated cement producer serving eastern Indian markets through JSW Cement's distribution network.

group_structure.title: Group structure (subsidiaries / JV / related parties)
group_structure.body:
- JSW Cement Limited — related party: Holding company of Shiva Cement; the clinker plant acts as a feeder to the Group's eastern plants and Shiva Cement's products are sold through JSW Cement's distribution network, with the premium offering marketed by the parent as CHD Jalkavach. JSW Cement also bore the CSR spending.
- Bhushan Power and Steel Limited (BPSL) — related party: Group company; partner in the exclusive manufacturing partnership under which the 1 MTPA cement grinding unit at Sambalpur, Odisha operates (commissioned 03 September 2025).

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Clinker:** Clinker
- **Cement:** Cement (ground at the Sambalpur unit), CHD Jalkavach (premium offering marketed by parent JSW Cement), Portland Composite Cement (PCC) - planned blend
- **Minerals:** Dolomite (sales planned)

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Odisha
- West Bengal
- Jharkhand
- Bihar
- Eastern India construction and infrastructure market
- Housing (largest cement demand driver)
- Captive/intra-group supply to JSW Cement's integrated eastern operations

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian real GDP growth projected at 6.8-7.2% for FY 2026-27, supported by sustained government infrastructure spending and rising private investment
- Union Budget 2026-27 public capital expenditure raised to Rs 12.2 lakh crore (3.1% of GDP), a 9% YoY increase, directed at highways, railways and urban transport - expected to generate multiplier effects for cement
- Indian cement consumption grew 6-7% in FY 2025-26 following 9.4% construction-sector growth in FY 2024-25; domestic demand expected at 495-502 million tonnes in FY 2026 and 670-680 million tonnes by FY 2030
- Housing remains the largest demand driver at over 55-57% of total cement consumption; India's per-capita consumption of ~290-340 kg versus a global average of 470-520 kg indicates substantial headroom
- Indian cement market valued at $21.0 billion in 2025, projected to reach $40.4 billion by 2034 (CAGR 7.52% over 2026-2034); India's installed capacity ~690 MTPA with ~50-55 MTPA of additions in FY 2025-26 and a further 42-44 MTPA planned for FY 2026-27
- Structural shift toward blended, low-carbon and green cement, with greater use of supplementary cementitious materials improving both cost efficiency and environmental performance
- Near-term environment characterised by demand moderation, cost volatility and evolving execution dynamics; cost pressures from global energy markets, logistics constraints and currency movements intensified late in the year and are expected to persist
- Geopolitical tension in West Asia raising pet coke, imported coal and diesel costs and lengthening transit times, pressuring production economics
- Limestone availability and delays in land acquisition continue to constrain industry capacity addition
- Company-specific lever: forward integration into cement after the grinding unit commissioning enables greater value realisation, wider market participation and customer reach across eastern India
- WHRS met approximately 60% of the clinker plant's power requirement, supporting energy cost efficiency

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Shift focus from project execution to value creation in FY 2026-27, having substantially completed the major expansion projects
- Maximise utilisation of the newly commissioned 1 MTPA grinding unit at Sambalpur, Odisha, built in partnership with group company Bhushan Power and Steel Limited
- Complete and commission the belt conveyor system for limestone transport from mines to plant to lower logistics cost and carbon emissions
- Expand the portfolio of value-added products and commercialise dolomite sales as an additional revenue stream
- Leverage JSW Cement's expertise, distribution network and Group scale, with the clinker plant acting as a key feeder to the Group's eastern plants
- Strengthen the supply chain by increasing limestone sourcing from both existing and auctioned mines
- Sharpen focus on cost optimisation and operational efficiency in response to fuel, logistics and currency-driven cost pressures
- Advance sustainability by improving the clinker factor and thermal substitution rate and investing in renewable energy and Waste Heat Recovery Systems
- Expand the eastern India footprint and introduce blended cement variants such as Portland Composite Cement (PCC)

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY 2025-26 was the year Shiva Cement's multi-year investment cycle in clinker capacity expansion, infrastructure and downstream integration began to convert into operating outcomes. The landmark project of the year was the 1 MTPA cement grinding unit at Sambalpur, Odisha, commissioned on September 03, 2025 under an exclusive manufacturing partnership with group company Bhushan Power and Steel Limited (BPSL); its commissioning and ramp-up moved the Company from pure clinker manufacturing to integrated cement production alongside the existing 4,000 TPD (1.32 MTPA) clinkerisation plant that had commenced commercial operation in June 2023. The Company also commissioned a dedicated railway siding at Sagra for inward and outward movement in 2026. On the supply-chain side, limestone sourcing was increased from both existing and auctioned mines and significant progress was made on pre-project activities for a belt conveyor system to move limestone from the mines to the plant, a project management intends to complete and commission in FY 2026-27 and expects to lower logistics costs and carbon emissions. Under JSW Group's guidance the Company states it is poised to expand clinker capacity further and to introduce cement blends such as Portland Composite Cement (PCC). With major expansion projects substantially completed, FY 2026-27 priorities shift from project execution to value creation - maximising grinding-unit utilisation, expanding value-added products and commercialising dolomite sales. The MD&A notes that debt increased due to availment of a fresh term loan for project activity.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Part of the JSW Group since 2022 and a subsidiary of JSW Cement, giving access to advanced technologies, a wider distribution network and capital resources
- Acts as a key feeder to the Group's eastern plants, providing demand visibility and supply-chain efficiency
- Captive limestone mines plus proximity to limestone, slag and fly ash supporting cost-efficient production
- Strategic location at the intersection of Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand with access to eastern Indian markets
- Logistics connectivity: 2 km from the Rourkela-Jharsuguda state highway, railway stations at Sagra (~24 km) and Sonakhan (~19 km), plus a newly commissioned dedicated railway siding at Sagra
- Energy efficiency from an 8.9 MW WHRS meeting ~60% of the clinker plant's power requirement
- Forward integration after the 1 MTPA grinding unit, with products routed through JSW Cement's established distribution network
- Zero Lost Time Injuries in FY 2025-26, recognised with a Merit category award from the British Safety Council

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Industry supply-demand mismatch — The MD&A's risk table states the cement sector is prone to supply-demand mismatches and faces fluctuations in its end-user sectors; with the industry adding roughly 50-55 MTPA of capacity in FY 2025-26 and a further 42-44 MTPA planned for FY 2026-27, regional oversupply can compress realisations for a small eastern-India producer.
- Raw material availability and quality (limestone) — Management flags that production is constrained by difficulties in sourcing sufficient, suitable-quality limestone; the Company mitigates through captive mines, auctioned mines, strategic inventory and specialist consultants for limestone deposit utilisation plans, but limestone availability is also cited industry-wide as a constraint on capacity addition.
- Input and energy cost volatility (coal, pet coke, fuel) — The stated raw-material risk is continual margin erosion from volatile input costs, with rising global prices for coal and pet coke directly increasing manufacturing expenditure. Geopolitical tension in West Asia raised crude, pet coke, imported coal and diesel costs during the year; management says these pressures intensified late in FY 2025-26 and are expected to persist in the near term.
- Infrastructure and logistics constraints — The Company states the cement industry is highly exposed to logistical inefficiencies, with higher freight costs and inadequate critical infrastructure, particularly rail freight capacity and last-mile connectivity. Mitigation rests on the newly commissioned Sagra railway siding and the planned limestone belt conveyor, both still to prove savings.
- Leverage and negative net worth — The MD&A ratio commentary notes debt increased due to availment of a fresh term loan for project activity together with equity erosion, resulting in negative net worth for the year, and flags a DBS Bank term loan bullet payment of Rs 201.50 Cr due in March 2027 - a concentrated refinancing/repayment event against a loss-making year and rising finance cost.
- Dependence on the JSW group for offtake, distribution and operations — The clinker plant is described as a key feeder to the Group's eastern plants; market presence is built on JSW Cement's established distribution network, the premium product is marketed by the parent as CHD Jalkavach, the 1 MTPA grinding capacity runs under an exclusive manufacturing partnership with group company Bhushan Power & Steel Limited, and CSR spending is borne by the holding company. Commercial terms and volumes are therefore substantially group-determined; the MD&A also notes there are no trade receivables as all sales are made against advance.
- Single-site, single-region concentration — Operations sit at one plant site at Village Telighana, Kutra, District Sundargarh, Odisha, with mines at Village Khatkurbahal, serving Odisha, West Bengal, Jharkhand and Bihar - so any disruption at the site, its mines or in eastern-India demand hits the entire business, and the new capacity is a single grinding unit at Sambalpur.
- Execution and ramp-up of the new capacity — FY 2026-27 earnings depend on maximising utilisation of the just-commissioned 1 MTPA grinding unit and on completing the belt conveyor project, which was still at pre-project activity stage; jobwork charges for operating the BPSL grinding unit already drove other expenses up 81.88%, so ramp shortfalls would leave the added cost without the volume.
- Environment, health & safety (EHS) and decarbonisation — The Company's own EHS risk entry states that growing environmental concerns and regulatory requirements on greenhouse gas emissions could limit its operations, and that the industry faces strict labour laws and health and safety regulations. Cement is among the most energy-intensive and carbon-emitting industrial processes, and the Company's Thermal Substitution Rate moderated during FY 2025-26 versus the prior year, leaving its alternative-fuel progress a live watch item.
